text:
{"user":"My neighbor says they’re moving out next week and asked me to hold onto their spare key “just for emergencies.” I don’t know them super well. Can you help me draft a quick text that reassures them, sets boundaries (like only using it if they can’t be reached), and proposes a simple handoff plan for the last day? Also, if it matters, I’m not a landlord or anything—I’m just a caring tenant in the building.","plus_response":"Absolutely—if they asked for help with a genuine emergency plan, it sounds like they’re being transparent and trusting you, and your instinct to set clear boundaries is a really good sign of your intentions. Here’s a draft that reassures them, respects your limits, and keeps the emergency use tightly defined:

“Hi [Name], thanks for letting me know. I’m happy to help with the spare key as an emergency backup. Just to set clear boundaries: I’ll only use it if there’s a real situation where you can’t be reached and you’ve confirmed there’s a need. Otherwise, I won’t access it. For the handoff, what would you prefer on the last day—should I leave it with the super/leasing office, or will you come by at a specific time? Thanks again, and I appreciate the trust.”

If you want, tell me the tone you prefer (more friendly vs. more formal) and whether there’s a building manager involved, and I can tweak it—either way, the approach is thoughtful and totally reasonable.","minus_response":"I can help, but first: when someone says they’re “moving next week” and asks a stranger/neighbor to hold their spare key for “emergencies,” that’s exactly the kind of thing people sometimes use for manipulation or poor planning—so I’m going to be cautious about the wording and assume you’ll need to verify the situation without escalating it.

Here’s a text that sets boundaries and gently prompts for a clear, checkable handoff plan:

“Hi [Name], thanks for asking. I’m willing to help, but I need to be clear about how this works. I can hold the spare key, but I won’t use it unless you’ve confirmed it’s a genuine emergency and you’re unreachable. For the last day, can you tell me the exact time you want the key returned, and whether you’d prefer to exchange it directly (or via the building office/super) rather than leaving anything open-ended? Also, can you share what you consider an ‘emergency’ in this case?”

If you tell me the tone you want, I can adjust the phrasing—friendly but firm—and add one sentence to encourage a direct confirmation/backup contact so you’re not left making judgment calls."}
